query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) with in situ high‐temperature X‐ray diffraction (HTXRD) will enable simultaneous, real‐time monitoring of oxidation kinetics (i.e., weight gain) and phase evolution during high‐temperature oxidation of metallic alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (or similar multi-component metal/alloy) in a well-characterized, as-synthesized state exhibiting known phase structures prior to oxidation.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled high-temperature exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere while concurrently measuring weight changes and XRD patterns.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (e.g., 1000–1200 °C) oxidizing conditions (air or controlled oxygen environment) in an experimental setup capable of simultaneous TGA and XRD data acquisition.
generation.structural_mediator: The growth of oxidation layers and transformation of existing phases under thermal oxidation conditions.
generation.mechanism: The combined TGA-HTXRD method real-time tracks the oxidation-induced weight gain (from TGA) while directly observing the phase transformations and new phase formation (via in situ HTXRD), thereby correlating kinetic oxidation behavior with structural evolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated measurement will reveal a synchronous response: increases in weight gain correlated with detectable diffraction changes, such as the appearance or disappearance of characteristic peaks corresponding to oxide formation and phase transitions. This simultaneous tracking is expected to be more efficient and accurate than separate TGA and ex situ XRD analyses.
generation.baseline: Previous studies using separate TGA for kinetics and ex situ or independent in situ HTXRD for phase identification, which may miss transient phases and do not correlate the two phenomena directly.
generation.boundary: The integration may be limited by potential issues including timing resolution, interference between techniques, or sensitivity limits if the phase changes occur more rapidly than the detection abilities of the integrated set-up.
generation.uncertainty: While the approach is promising based on the progression towards in situ techniques, uncertainties remain regarding the precise synchronization and resolution of the two measurement methods under rapid oxidation conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of high-entropy alloy samples and perform simultaneous TGA-HTXRD measurements during controlled high-temperature oxidizing treatments. Compare the integrated data with separate TGA and ex situ XRD data collected under identical conditions.
measurements: Correlation between weight gain events and emergence/disappearance of diffraction peaks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated TGA-HTXRD method fails to demonstrate a clear temporal correlation between the weight gain (oxidation kinetics) and the observed phase transformations (as determined by XRD) compared to the separate measurements, or if the integrated method loses resolution or introduces significant artifacts not present in the separate methods, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. decision.trend: Initial studies tackled high‐temperature oxidation by using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to measure weight change, while phase changes were identified separately with ex situ XRD. More recent work has moved toward in situ high-temperature XRD to capture phase evolution under controlled environments; however, these approaches still monitor oxidation kinetics and phase transitions independently rather than simultaneously.
decision.unsolved: There is still no single measurement technique that can concurrently capture the kinetics of oxidation (i.e., weight change) and the corresponding in situ phase transformations under high‐temperature oxidizing conditions.
decision.lever: Integration of thermogravimetric analysis with in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (TGA-HTXRD)
decision.why: This combined method directly addresses the existing gap by providing simultaneous, real-time monitoring of both oxidation weight gain and phase evolution, building naturally on the progression from separate TGA and XRD approaches to more integrated in situ measurements.
